title: 'Iron of itself draws a man on': removing the arms
greek: αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐφέλκεται ἄνδρα σίδηρος (autos gar ephelketai andra sidēros)
short: The cover story for removing the weapons from the hall ends with a proverb about iron tempting men to violence.
body: Odysseus and Telemachus clear the hall of arms so that the suitors will be unarmed when the moment comes; the excuse is that smoke has spoiled them and that weapons within reach invite drunken quarrels. The scene repeats almost verbatim instructions already given at 16.281-98, and Monro gives a long account of the problem: ancient and modern critics suspected the Book XVI passage, Kirchhoff defended it, and Monro suspects both. Among his arguments is the proverb itself. Homeric weapons are of bronze, and 'iron' as a general word for weapons belongs to a later age, when iron had become the usual metal; the advice also assumes that men did not normally carry arms, though the suitors wear swords. Thucydides remembered a time when 'all Greece went armed' (1.6.1). Whatever its origin, the line has become one of the best-known Greek sayings about the temptation of weapons.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 19.1-50

title: Athena's golden lamp
greek: πάροιθε δὲ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη χρύσεον λύχνον ἔχουσα φάος περικαλλὲς ἐποίει (paroithe de Pallas Athēnē chruseon luchnon echousa phaos perikalles epoiei)
short: Invisible Athena lights the way; the walls glow 'as with blazing fire', and Odysseus tells his son this is the way of the gods.
body: Telemachus sees the beams, walls and pillars shining and guesses that 'some god is within'. Odysseus silences him: 'this is the way (dikē) of the gods that hold Olympus'. Divine radiance is a regular sign of epiphany in Greek poetry (compare Demeter's light filling the house in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter 188-9, 275-80), and the scene fulfils, unseen by the suitors, Eurymachus' mocking claim that the beggar came 'not without the gods' (18.351-5). Monro notes that the lamp (luchnos) is otherwise unknown to Homer, who lights houses with torches and braziers, and that both the word and the scansion of chruseon look late; he takes this as further evidence that the arms-removal scene is a later addition. Readers who do not share his analytic premises still find the scene's quiet strangeness effective.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 19.1-50 and 19.34

title: Icmalius and Penelope's chair
greek: κλισίην ... δινωτὴν ἐλέφαντι καὶ ἀργύρῳ, ἥν ποτε τέκτων ποίησ᾽ Ἰκμάλιος (klisiēn ... dinōtēn elephanti kai argurōi, hēn pote tektōn poiēs' Ikmalios)
short: Penelope sits in a chair inlaid with ivory and silver, with an attached footstool, made by a named craftsman found only here.
body: Named makers of objects are rare in Homer and give an object a history: Tychius, 'best of leather-workers', made Ajax's shield (Il. 7.219-23), and Hephaestus made the sceptre of Agamemnon. Icmalius is otherwise unknown. Monro explains dinōtēn as 'turned', with ivory and silver carried round the wood-work, and notes that the klisiē here is a chair rather than a couch. The chair sets the scene for the long interview that follows. Penelope is formally enthroned by the fire, with a fleece on her seat, while the beggar is given a lesser chair opposite her (19.97-101). Their conversation, the longest exchange between husband and wife before the recognition, takes place across this careful arrangement of status.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 19.55-6

title: Penelope compared to a just king (a 'reverse simile')
greek: ὥς τέ τευ ἢ βασιλῆος ἀμύμονος, ὅς τε θεουδὴς ... εὐδικίας ἀνέχῃσι (hōs te teu ē basilēos amumonos, hos te theoudēs ... eudikias anechēisi)
short: Odysseus likens Penelope's fame to that of a god-fearing king under whom land, flocks and sea prosper: a woman praised in a king's terms.
body: The picture of the just king whose rule makes the earth bear grain, the trees fruit, the flocks young and the sea fish is close to Hesiod's description of the just city (Works and Days 225-37). Monro thought lines 109-14 Hesiodic in style and perhaps a fragment of early gnomic poetry; he also notes that fishing as a source of wealth is unusual in Homer. Helene Foley drew attention to a series of 'reverse similes' in the Odyssey, in which men are compared to women and women to men, and placed this one at their centre: Penelope, holding the house together in her husband's absence, is praised in the language of kingship. The compliment is double, since it also describes the role that Odysseus himself must reclaim.

sources.cite: Helene P. Foley, '"Reverse Similes" and Sex Roles in the Odyssey', Arethusa 11 (1978) 7-26
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 19.109-14

title: 'Not sprung from an oak or a stone'
greek: οὐ γὰρ ἀπὸ δρυός ἐσσι παλαιφάτου οὐδ᾽ ἀπὸ πέτρης (ou gar apo druos essi palaiphatou oud' apo petrēs)
short: A proverbial phrase meaning 'you must have parents like everyone else': Penelope insists on knowing the stranger's lineage.
body: The expression was already old when the Odyssey was composed. Hector uses a version of it in the Iliad (22.126-8), and Hesiod's narrator breaks off with 'but why this talk about oak or stone?' (Theogony 35). Socrates in Plato's Apology (34d) quotes the Homeric phrase to say that he too has a family. Monro takes the sense here to be 'you are not of some obscure origin', 'not a nobody', and warns against tying it too closely to myths of men born from trees or stones, though such myths existed (for example the bronze race born from ash trees in Hesiod, Works and Days 145, or the stones thrown by Deucalion and Pyrrha). Whatever its origins, the proverb presses the point Odysseus has tried to avoid: a stranger in the Greek world is defined by his father and his city.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 19.163

title: Crete, 'ninety cities' and many tongues
greek: ἐν δ᾽ ἄνθρωποι πολλοί, ἀπειρέσιοι, καὶ ἐννήκοντα πόληες· ἄλλη δ᾽ ἄλλων γλῶσσα μεμιγμένη (en d' anthrōpoi polloi, apeiresioi, kai ennēkonta polēes; allē d' allōn glōssa memigmenē)
short: Odysseus' description of Crete: ninety cities and a mixture of languages spoken by Achaeans, Eteocretans, Cydonians, Dorians and Pelasgians.
body: The Iliad calls Crete 'hundred-citied' (2.649); ancient scholars noticed the difference, and Strabo (10.4.15) reports Ephorus' explanation that ten cities were destroyed after the Trojan War. The list of peoples is precious ethnographic evidence. Monro explains the Eteocretans ('true Cretans') as the original inhabitants, later found in eastern Crete around Praesus, where inscriptions in a non-Greek language survived into historical times; the Cydonians lived in the west (compare 3.292); the Pelasgians appear in the Iliad as Trojan allies and were said by Herodotus (1.57) to speak a non-Greek tongue. Strabo (10.4.6) quotes these lines and discusses which peoples were Greek. The mixture suits Odysseus' lying persona: Crete is famous, distant and complicated enough for any story to be plausible.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 19.175-7

title: 'Dorians of waving plumes' (trichaikes)
greek: Δωριέες τε τριχάϊκες (Dōrieës te trichaïkes)
short: The only mention of Dorians in Homer; their unique epithet probably means 'with tossing hair', though ancients linked it to their three tribes.
body: The Dorians, who dominated the Peloponnese and Crete in historical times, are otherwise absent from Homer, and their appearance here is a well-known puzzle. Monro thought it hard to identify them with the historical Dorians and considered a local people named from a place called Dorion, while noting the Iliad's account of Rhodes settled in three divisions (2.668). The epithet trichaikes is unique. Monro derives it from thrix ('hair') and aïssō ('to dart, to toss'), 'with flowing or tossing hair', which Murray renders 'of waving plumes'. A Hesiodic fragment quoted in LSJ already explains it by popular etymology from tricha, 'in three parts', because the Dorians divided a threefold land far from their homeland; later writers linked the word with the three Dorian tribes. The line is a small window on how epic language was reinterpreted by later Greeks.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 19.175-7 (Dorians and τριχάϊκες)
Hesiod, fragment on the Dorians cited in LSJ s.v. τριχάϊκες (fr. 191 Rzach)

title: Minos, 'nine years' king and companion of Zeus
greek: ἐννέωρος βασίλευε Διὸς μεγάλου ὀαριστής (enneōros basileue Dios megalou oaristēs)
short: An old crux: Minos ruled Cnossus 'at nine years old', 'for nine years' or 'every ninth year', as the familiar companion of great Zeus.
body: Enneōros literally means 'of nine seasons'. Monro sets out the options: 'nine years old', which gives a pointless marvel; 'for nine years', which goes against the usage of such adjectives; or a phrase meaning that Minos ruled 'after nine years' or 'in the fullness of time', with nine as a round number. Plato took it as a reference to Minos' regular visits to the cave of Zeus: in the Laws (624a-b) and the Minos (319b-320b) he says Minos went every ninth year to converse with Zeus and brought back the laws of Crete. Oaristēs, 'familiar companion, one who converses intimately', suits that reading. Odysseus makes his false self a grandson of Minos and brother of Idomeneus, the Cretan leader at Troy, a fiction of the highest possible status.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 19.179

title: Aethon, Odysseus' false name
greek: ἐμοὶ δ᾽ ὄνομα κλυτὸν Αἴθων (emoi d' onoma kluton Aithōn)
short: The disguised hero calls himself Aethon, 'Blazing', a name also used for burning hunger: a fitting alias for a man driven by his belly.
body: Aithōn means 'burning, fiery', and by extension 'tawny' or 'flashing'; it is used of metal, of lions and of oxen (Odysseus has just imagined 'tawny' oxen, aithōnes, at 18.372). In the Hesiodic Catalogue of Women the impious Erysichthon, punished with insatiable hunger, was nicknamed Aithon (fr. 43a Merkelbach-West), so the name may hint at the beggar's ravenous gaster. It is the name Odysseus gives his false Cretan self here (in Book 24 he will call himself Eperitus, 24.306), and he calls it 'famous', an irony in a poem obsessed with the hero's real name and fame. The story attached to it, that Aethon entertained Odysseus in Crete when storms drove him there on the way to Troy, is designed to let Odysseus describe himself to his wife as a guest remembers a guest.

sources.cite: Hesiod, Catalogue of Women, Erysichthon called Aithon (fr. 43a Merkelbach-West)
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 19.184

title: Amnisus and the cave of Eilithyia
greek: στῆσε δ᾽ ἐν Ἀμνισῷ, ὅθι τε σπέος Εἰλειθυίης (stēse d' en Amnisōi, hothi te speos Eileithuiēs)
short: A real place: the harbour of Cnossus, with a cave sacred to Eilithyia, goddess of childbirth, attested already in Linear B.
body: Monro identifies Amnisus as the ancient harbour of Cnossus, and Strabo (10.4.8) mentions it as Minos' port, with a sanctuary of Eileithyia. Eilithyia (in the Iliad also plural, the Eilithyiai, 11.270-1, 16.187) is the goddess who presides over birth. The site is one of the most striking links between Homer and the Bronze Age. A Linear B tablet from Cnossos (KN Gg 705) records an offering of honey to Eleuthia at a-mi-ni-so, Amnisos, and the cave itself, with cult remains from Minoan times, was excavated in the twentieth century. The detail lends Odysseus' lie the texture of real geography: it is exactly the sort of precise local knowledge that makes his tales 'like the truth' (19.203).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 19.188
Linear B tablet KN Gg 705 (honey for e-re-u-ti-ja at a-mi-ni-so), in M. Ventris and J. Chadwick, Documents in Mycenaean Greek (2nd ed., Cambridge, 1973)

title: The melting-snow simile
greek: τήκετο δὲ χρώς. ὡς δὲ χιὼν κατατήκετ᾽ ἐν ἀκροπόλοισιν ὄρεσσιν (tēketo de chrōs. hōs de chiōn katatēket' en akropoloisin oressin)
short: Penelope weeps at the lying tale as mountain snow melts and swells the rivers: 'he made the many falsehoods of his tale seem like the truth'.
body: The line introducing the simile is one of the poem's key statements about fiction: Odysseus 'made many lies like to true things' (pseudea polla legōn etumoisin homoia), words echoed by Hesiod's Muses (Theogony 27). The simile then turns the effect of the lie into landscape. Monro notes a shift in the verb tēkō, from 'her skin was wet' to 'melt' in the comparison, and a puzzle in the winds: the snow is laid down by the West Wind and thawed by the East, the reverse of what we expect, so that some have proposed exchanging the names. In the Iliad Odysseus' words fall 'like winter snowflakes' (3.222); here the snow of his speech melts into his wife's tears. The image prepares the stark contrast that follows, between her streaming face and his fixed eyes.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 19.203-8 and 19.206

title: Eyes 'like horn or iron'
greek: ὀφθαλμοὶ δ᾽ ὡς εἰ κέρα ἕστασαν ἠὲ σίδηρος ἀτρέμας ἐν βλεφάροισι (ophthalmoi d' hōs ei kera hestasan ēe sidēros atremas en blepharoisi)
short: Odysseus pities his weeping wife but keeps his eyes motionless, as hard as horn or iron, hiding his tears 'with guile'.
body: Horn and iron are images of hardness and immobility. The contrast with the melting snow of the previous simile is exact: she dissolves, he stays fixed. Yet the narrator insists that 'in his heart he had pity'; the hardness is a mask, not insensibility. Earlier in the poem Odysseus could not control his tears when the bard Demodocus sang of Troy and had to hide his face in his cloak (8.83-92, 8.521-31). Now his self-mastery is complete, and that very control is what Penelope cannot see through. The same language returns when Eurycleia promises to be silent 'as hard stone or iron' (19.494), and when Penelope herself is called 'iron-hearted' for her caution at the recognition (23.172).

title: The golden brooch: hound and fawn
greek: περόνη χρυσοῖο τέτυκτο αὐλοῖσιν διδύμοισι· πάροιθε δὲ δαίδαλον ἦεν· ἐν προτέροισι πόδεσσι κύων ἔχε ποικίλον ἐλλόν (peronē chrusoio tetukto auloisin didumoisi ... en proteroisi podessi kuōn eche poikilon ellon)
short: To prove he met Odysseus, the beggar describes a gold brooch showing a hound pinning a struggling fawn, and Penelope recognises her own gift.
body: This is a test of tokens (sēmata), and Odysseus passes it by describing the clothes Penelope herself gave him. Monro explains the auloi as the twin sheaths into which the pins of the brooch fit, and the verb laō as a hunting term for a dog 'gripping' its prey; the marvel is that inanimate gold seems alive and moving, as in the description of Akhilleus' shield (Il. 18.548-9). The image carries more than technical interest. A hound seizing a fawn recalls Menelaus' simile of the lion who returns to kill the fawns in his lair (4.335-40, repeated at 17.126-31), and it follows closely on the story of the old hound Argos. The brooch is an emblem of the hunter-husband who is about to fall on the suitors.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 19.225-31

anchor: the skin of a dried onion
title: A tunic like the skin of a dried onion
greek: οἷόν τε κρομύοιο λοπὸν κάτα ἰσχαλέοιο (hoion te kromuoio lopon kata ischaleoio)
short: Odysseus' tunic shone as smooth and soft as the papery skin of a dried onion, 'and it glistened like the sun'.
body: The homely comparison surprises in a list of luxury goods, but it is precise: the outer skin of a dry onion is thin, smooth and lustrous. Monro discusses the grammar (whether the onion's peel lies 'over' it or the tunic shines 'like' the peel) and cites the archaeologists Tsountas and Manatt, who took the garment to be a fitted linen shirt, clinging 'like an onion peel', in contrast to the loose woollen garments of everyday dress. A fragment of the comic poet Theopompus refers to the passage. Penelope's tears at this description show that the detail, not the grand language, is what convinces: she 'recognised the sure tokens' (19.250).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 19.233 (citing Tsountas and Manatt, The Mycenaean Age, p. 161)

title: Eurybates, Odysseus' herald
greek: Εὐρυβάτης δ᾽ ὄνομ᾽ ἔσκε (Eurubatēs d' onom' eske)
short: The beggar adds a lifelike portrait of Odysseus' herald: round-shouldered, dark-skinned, curly-haired, and like-minded with his master.
body: Eurybates is a figure from the Iliad: an Ithacan herald who follows Odysseus and picks up the cloak he throws off as he runs to stop the army's flight (Il. 2.183-4). A herald of the same name serves Agamemnon (Il. 1.320) and goes with Odysseus on the embassy to Akhilleus (Il. 9.170). The physical description here is unusually specific for Homer and has an air of real memory; Monro records an ancient variant reading in its first words. The herald is honoured 'because he was like-minded' (artia ēidē) with Odysseus, a phrase that anticipates the poem's ideal of like-mindedness (homophrosunē) between husband and wife (6.181-5). Penelope has now been given tokens of dress and companions, and she accepts the stranger as a true witness.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), critical note on 19.246

title: Kakoilion: 'Evil-Ilios, not to be named'
greek: ᾤχετ᾽ ἐποψόμενος Κακοΐλιον οὐκ ὀνομαστήν (ōichet' epopsomenos Kakoïlion ouk onomastēn)
short: Penelope coins a compound of 'evil' and 'Ilios' for the city that took her husband, a place whose very name she will not say.
body: The compound joins kakos ('evil') to the name of Troy; ouk onomastēn means 'not to be named', a place of ill omen. Penelope uses the line twice in this book (19.260, 19.597) and again in Book XXIII (23.19). It belongs to a small group of name-compounds of reproach in Homer, such as Hector's Dysparis, 'evil Paris' (Il. 3.39), and the suitors' Iros Airos, 'un-Irus' (18.73). For Penelope Troy is not a place of glory, as it is for the singers who celebrate the war, but the cause of twenty years of grief. The word sums up the Odyssey's view of the war from home.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 18.73 (on such privative compounds)

title: The scar and Eurycleia's recognition
greek: αὐτίκα δ᾽ ἔγνω οὐλήν, τήν ποτέ μιν σῦς ἤλασε λευκῷ ὀδόντι (autika d' egnō oulēn, tēn pote min sus ēlase leukōi odonti)
short: Washing his feet, the old nurse feels the boar-scar; the narrative stops for a long flashback before she lets the foot fall into the basin.
body: Odysseus asked to be washed only by an old woman and turned away from the fire too late. The moment of recognition is suspended for some seventy lines while the poet tells how the scar was got. Erich Auerbach made this digression the starting point of Mimesis (1946): Homer, he argued, brings everything into a uniformly lit foreground, so that the flashback is told with the same fullness as the present, in contrast with the 'fraught with background' style of the binding of Isaac in Genesis. Later critics have stressed instead that the digression follows Eurycleia's memory and builds suspense. Monro reports that Kirchhoff and Wilamowitz condemned 395-466 as an interpolation, but finds no sign of late language, and he defends Odysseus' choice of an old nurse by the manners of the age. The scar recurs as a token at 21.217-21, 23.73-7 and 24.331-5.

sources.cite: Erich Auerbach, Mimesis (Bern, 1946; trans. W. R. Trask, Princeton, 1953), ch. 1, 'Odysseus' Scar'
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 19.346-8, 19.389 and 19.395-466

title: Autolycus, master of theft and oaths
greek: ὃς ἀνθρώπους ἐκέκαστο κλεπτοσύνῃ θ᾽ ὅρκῳ τε· θεὸς δέ οἱ αὐτὸς ἔδωκεν Ἑρμείας (hos anthrōpous ekekasto kleptosunēi th' horkōi te; theos de hoi autos edōken Hermeias)
short: Odysseus' maternal grandfather, whose name suggests 'the wolf himself', excelled in stealing and in tricky oaths, a gift from Hermes.
body: Autolycus is the father of Odysseus' mother Anticleia (11.85). His skill 'in oaths' does not mean perjury in a simple sense but cleverness in swearing, saying what is literally true while deceiving. The gift comes from Hermes, the god of thieves and tricksters, whom Autolycus honours with sacrifices; in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes the infant god steals Apollo's cattle and swears ambiguous oaths to escape blame. The Iliad remembers Autolycus as the thief who broke into Amyntor's house and stole the boar's-tusk helmet that Odysseus later wears (Il. 10.261-71). The grandfather explains the grandson: Odysseus' cunning and his gift for plausible lies are an inheritance on his mother's side, as his scar is a mark received in his mother's family's country.

title: The naming of Odysseus (odyssamenos)
greek: πολλοῖσιν γὰρ ἐγώ γε ὀδυσσάμενος τόδ᾽ ἱκάνω ... τῷ δ᾽ Ὀδυσεὺς ὄνομ᾽ ἔστω ἐπώνυμον (polloisin gar egō ge odussamenos tod' hikanō ... tōi d' Odyseus onom' estō epōnumon)
short: Autolycus names his grandson from the verb odyssomai, 'to be angry, to hate': the child is to bear the name of his grandfather's many quarrels.
body: Autolycus says he comes 'having been angered (odyssamenos) with many, men and women', and so the child shall be Odysseus. Monro takes the participle as active, 'a man of many quarrels', and rejects the passive sense 'hated by many', which has no support for this verb. The same verb, however, is used throughout the poem of the gods' hostility to Odysseus: Athena asks Zeus why he is 'so angry' (ōdusao) with him (1.62), and Poseidon is 'wroth' with him (5.340, 5.423). The name thus points in both directions, to one who gives and receives odium, 'the man of wrath'. George Dimock's essay 'The Name of Odysseus' made this ambiguity central to reading the poem, and Jenny Strauss Clay developed it in her study of Athena's anger. The name's meaning is revealed exactly when its bearer's identity is discovered.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 19.407
George E. Dimock, 'The Name of Odysseus', Hudson Review 9 (1956) 52-70
Jenny Strauss Clay, The Wrath of Athena: Gods and Men in the Odyssey (Princeton, 1983)

anchor: they went forth to the hunt
title: The boar hunt on Parnassus
greek: βάν ῥ᾽ ἴμεν ἐς θήρην ... Παρνησὸν ... σῦς μέγας (ban rh' imen es thērēn ... Parnēson ... sus megas)
short: As a young man Odysseus visits his mother's kin and joins his first boar hunt, killing the boar but taking a wound above the knee.
body: The episode moves from naming to adolescence. Odysseus comes to Parnassus to claim the gifts Autolycus promised at his birth, is welcomed by his mother's family (whom Monro identifies with the mētrōes, the maternal kin), and goes out at dawn with his uncles and the hounds. The description of the boar's lair, so thick that neither wind, sun nor rain could penetrate it, repeats lines describing the thicket where Odysseus himself sheltered in Scheria (5.478-85, as Monro notes). The young hero strikes first and is gored, then kills the beast; the uncles bind the wound and stop the blood with a charm. A first hunt, a first wound, gifts from the mother's brothers and a return home to tell the story have the shape of a coming of age, and the scar that results becomes the mark of identity by which the adult is known.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 19.410, 19.440-3 and 19.450

title: Stopping blood with a charm (epaoidē)
greek: ἐπαοιδῇ δ᾽ αἷμα κελαινὸν ἔσχεθον (epaoidēi d' haima kelainon eschethon)
short: The sons of Autolycus bind the wound skilfully and stop the bleeding with an incantation: the only healing spell in Homer.
body: Epaoidē (later epōidē, the source of English 'ode' and 'epode') is a song or spell sung over someone. In the Iliad wounds are treated with herbs, bandages and pressure, never with spells, so this detail stands out. Practical first aid and magic sit side by side here, as they did in Greek medicine for centuries: Pindar's Asclepius heals 'with gentle incantations' as well as drugs and surgery (Pythian 3.51-3), and in Plato's Charmides (155e-157b) Socrates offers a charm for headache that must be used with a herbal remedy. The charm suits the family of Autolycus, whose skills lie in words that work on the world. The scene also reminds us that the scar was the result of skilful treatment, which is why it healed into a lasting mark.

anchor: she touched the chin of Odysseus
title: Eurycleia touches his chin; Odysseus seizes her throat
greek: ἁψαμένη δὲ γενείου Ὀδυσσῆα προσέειπεν (hapsamenē de geneiou Odussēa proseeipen)
short: The nurse's tender gesture, also the gesture of a suppliant, is met by force: Odysseus grips her throat and threatens her life to keep the secret.
body: Touching the chin is part of the ritual of supplication, as when Thetis clasps Zeus' knees and reaches up to his chin (Il. 1.500-2); John Gould's classic study treats such contact as the core of the suppliant's appeal. Here it is also an old nurse's caress, and she calls him 'dear child'. Joy and grief seize her at once (19.471), and she turns toward Penelope, whose attention Athena has deflected. Odysseus' reaction is shockingly violent: he takes her by the throat, pulls her close and warns that he will not spare her when he kills the other women. Eurycleia promises to be as silent as stone or iron, and offers to name the disloyal maids; he refuses, saying he will find them out himself. The scene shows how close recognition comes to ruining the plan, a point Monro makes in defending its place in the poem.

title: The nightingale simile: Pandareus' daughter and Itylus
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτε Πανδαρέου κούρη, χλωρηῒς ἀηδών ... παῖδ᾽ ὀλοφυρομένη Ἴτυλον φίλον (hōs d' hote Pandareou kourē, chlōrēïs aēdōn ... paid' olophuromenē Itulon philon)
short: Penelope compares her wavering mind to the nightingale's shifting song of lament for Itylus, the son she killed unwittingly.
body: The daughter of Pandareus is Aedon, whose name means 'nightingale'. According to the story preserved in the scholia (and attributed to Pherecydes), she was the wife of Zethus of Thebes and, envying her sister-in-law Niobe's many children, meant to kill one of them but killed her own son Itylus by mistake; the gods turned her into the nightingale, forever mourning. The better-known Athenian version tells of Procne and Itys. Monro explains chlōrēis as 'of the greenwood' rather than 'green-coloured', and suggests the name Itylus imitates the bird's call. Penelope's comparison works on two levels: the trilling, shifting song mirrors a mind that 'sways to and fro' between staying and remarrying, and the image of a mother who destroys her son darkly reflects her fear for Telemachus, whose inheritance the suitors are eating.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 19.518 and 19.522
Scholia on Odyssey 19.518 (the Aedon story, attributed to Pherecydes)

title: Penelope's dream of the geese and the eagle
greek: χῆνές μοι κατὰ οἶκον ἐείκοσι πυρὸν ἔδουσιν ... ἐλθὼν δ᾽ ἐξ ὄρεος μέγας αἰετὸς (chēnes moi kata oikon eeikosi puron edousin ... elthōn d' ex oreos megas aietos)
short: An eagle kills Penelope's twenty pet geese, then speaks: the geese are the suitors, the eagle her husband. Yet in the dream she weeps for the geese.
body: The dream interprets itself: the eagle returns, perches on the roof-beam and explains, in a human voice, that it is Odysseus and the geese are the suitors. Odysseus agrees that no other meaning is possible. The omen closely resembles the sign at Sparta, where an eagle seized a goose and Helen read it as Odysseus' return (15.160-78). What has fascinated modern readers is Penelope's grief: she enjoys watching the geese and weeps when they die. Psychoanalytic critics such as George Devereux read this as an unconscious attachment to the suitors' attention; Joseph Russo, in a study of dream, fantasy and intuition in Books XIX-XX, sees it as the expression of mixed and partly hidden feelings at a moment of crisis, without making Penelope disloyal. The number twenty matches the years of Odysseus' absence, though the text does not draw the link.

sources.cite: Joseph Russo, 'Interview and Aftermath: Dream, Fantasy, and Intuition in Odyssey 19 and 20', American Journal of Philology 103 (1982) 4-18

title: The gates of horn and ivory
greek: δοιαὶ γάρ τε πύλαι ἀμενηνῶν εἰσὶν ὀνείρων· αἱ μὲν γὰρ κεράεσσι τετεύχαται, αἱ δ᾽ ἐλέφαντι (doiai gar te pulai amenēnōn eisin oneirōn; hai men gar keraessi teteuchatai, hai d' elephanti)
short: True dreams come through a gate of horn, deceptive ones through a gate of ivory: an image built on two Greek puns.
body: Penelope doubts her own dream. Dreams, she says, are 'shadowy' (amenēnoi, 'without force') and pass through two gates. Monro notes the plays on words: ivory (elephas) suggests elephairomai, 'to cheat, to deceive', and horn (keras) suggests krainō, 'to bring to pass, to fulfil'. The image was taken up by later writers, notably Plato's Charmides (173a) and Virgil, who ends Aeneid VI by sending Aeneas and the Sibyl out of the underworld through the ivory gate of false dreams (6.893-8), a choice that has been endlessly debated. In the Odyssey the irony is plain: Penelope dismisses as false a dream that is true, while the man who could confirm it sits before her.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 19.562-7

title: The contest of the bow and the twelve axes
greek: τοὺς πελέκεας, τοὺς κεῖνος ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἑοῖσιν ἵστασχ᾽ ἑξείης, δρυόχους ὥς, δώδεκα πάντας (tous pelekeas, tous keinos eni megaroisin heoisin histasch' hexeiēs, druochous hōs, dōdeka pantas)
short: Penelope decides to marry whoever can string Odysseus' bow and shoot through twelve axes set in a row: the device that leads to the slaughter.
body: How the shot worked is one of the oldest puzzles in Homer. Monro, following Helbig, explains the druochoi as the props on which a ship's keel rests while it is being built, so the axes stood upright in a straight line; the arrow must pass through openings in the axe-heads (or the rings at the end of the hafts), which had to be aligned to form a tube. He reviews forms of axe with such openings, including one from the Mycenaean tomb at Vapheio. The timing of Penelope's decision is equally debated. She announces the contest immediately after hearing that Odysseus is near and after a dream of his return. Philip Harsh argued that she has half-recognised her husband and is cooperating with him; others see an unconscious intuition, or simply despair. Odysseus' answer, that Odysseus will be home before any suitor strings the bow, approves her plan.
